newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - June 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - June 25.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- SING TAO -- The Chief Executive's Office announced post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa will be paid HK$330,000 (US$42,600) per month and, unlike Britain's colonial governors, will pay salary tax.

-- EXPRESS NEWS -- Chief Secretary Anson Chan said rumours she does not get along with Tung were unfounded. Although Tung and outgoing colonial Governor Chris Patten had different styles, Chan was confident she could adapt to working with a "new boss".
-- MING PAO -- China Telecom (Hong Kong) would be listed in Hong Kong and New York in September in a move aimed at raising US$2 billion.

-- Research showed most Hong Kong people aged 15 to 29 had not read the Basic Law, the territory's constitution after it reverts to Chinese rule on July 1. They said the handover had no special meaning to them and they were not excited about it.

-- Despite attempts by Chinese authorities to prevent huge crowds from rushing into Shenzhen, across the border from Hong Kong, during the handover period, hawkers were still selling fake "border passes" and smuggling people into the area. A bogus pass costs HK$150 and could be ready in 10 minutes.
-- TA KUNG PAO -- The U.S. Congress decided to renew China's Most Favoured Nation trade status and veteran politicians urged Washington to actively improve relations with Beijing.

-- APPLE DAILY -- Experts were puzzled over how the corpse a Hong Kong woman kept in her living room had not rotted after three years. Neighbours say they often saw the woman's children carrying home bags of ice.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- A government attempt to define anti-treason laws after the handover was scuppered by the incoming administration.

-- China securities regulators plan to increase the number of shares available to investors in Shenzhen and Shanghai in the last two trading days before the handover in an attempt to cool possible transition fever.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD - Democratic Party legislators rejected a compromise offered by the incoming government and insisted on using the balcony of the Legislative Council building to deliver "a manifesto and statement" early on July 1.
